Corpus shape matters as well as size

After an edit, the engine needs to read and parse the changed file. It also needs to check whether that edit changes where links in other files lead. Suppose Studio declares Workshop as an alias and a journal links to Workshop. Removing the alias changes the journal link's target even though the journal file is unchanged. The engine can reuse the journal's already-parsed text, but it must look up the link's target again.

The Goals page says the implementation should support concurrent writes to the same block using CRDTs as a front end to the cache. The Brief says a CRDT is a long-term direction and no MVP dependency. Resolve the two pages in the Brief's favor, and add a smaller step before either.
A Logseq-aware git merge driver before a CRDT
A Logseq-aware git merge driver before a CRDT

Agents work in git/worktrees on their own branches and merge through pull requests, per My/AI/Rule/Dev/Workflow/Git Worktree PR/Tmux. Two agents editing the same page meet at merge time, in git, as a textual conflict. A person edits in Logseq or nvim on main. The concurrency that exists is a merge problem, and git already has the extension point for it.

What a merge driver would do
A Logseq-aware git merge driver before a CRDT

Register a custom merge driver for pages/*.md and journals/*.md through .gitattributes. Git hands it the base, ours, and theirs versions; the driver parses all three as block trees, matches blocks by id:: when present and by parent path plus content otherwise, merges at block granularity, and leaves a textual conflict marker only inside a block both sides changed.

One SQLite file per checkout, under the XDG cache directory, holding pages, blocks, references, aliases, and a content hash for every source file. A command opens the file, compares each source file's size and modification time with the recorded ones the way git status does, rehashes only the files that changed, reparses those, and then re-resolves the links whose targets those files could have changed. Git's index has used the size-and-mtime shortcut for decades, so it is a known quantity.

After an edit the engine does two jobs: it re-reads the file that changed, and it re-checks links in other files whose target that change may have moved. 588fb79e docs: point nvim/Distro/LazyVim at LazyVim page removed alias:: [[nvim/Distro/LazyVim]] from the LazyVim page, and every [[nvim/Distro/LazyVim]] link in this garden changed target in a commit that edited none of the files holding those links.
